facts.statement: Pakasuchus fossils were discovered in the Galula Formation of southwestern Tanzania and formally described in 2010.
facts.quote: Fossils have been found in the Galula Formation of Rukwa Rift Basin of southwestern Tanzania, and were described in 2010 in the journal Nature.

facts.statement: A complete skeleton of Pakasuchus was found in 2008 by a team funded by the National Science Foundation and National Geographic Society.
facts.quote: A complete skeleton of Pakasuchus was found in 2008 in southwestern Tanzania by an international research team funded by the National Science Foundation and the National Geographic Society as part of the Rukwa Rift Basin Project.

facts.statement: The species name 'kapilimai' honors Saidi Kapilima, a leader of the excavation project.
facts.quote: The specific name honors Saidi Kapilima, one of the leaders of the Rukwa Rift Basin Project and who helped in the excavation of the specimens.

facts.statement: Researchers used CT scanning to examine the teeth of the Pakasuchus specimens.
facts.quote: The describers of the specimens used X-ray computed tomography scanning, or CT scanning, to image the teeth.

facts.statement: Pakasuchus is a notosuchian crocodyliform known for its mammal-like appearance and teeth adapted for chewing.
facts.quote: Pakasuchus is a genus of notosuchian crocodyliform distinguished by its unusual mammal-like appearance, including mammal-like teeth that would have given the animal the ability to chew.

facts.statement: Pakasuchus possessed long, slender legs and a dog-like nose.
facts.quote: It also had long, slender legs and a doglike nose.

facts.statement: Pakasuchus was approximately 50 cm long.
facts.quote: Pakasuchus was around 50 cm long.

facts.statement: Unlike modern crocodilians, Pakasuchus had heterodont teeth that varied in shape along its jaws.
facts.quote: Unlike living crocodilians, Pakasuchus had distinctive heterodont teeth that varied in shape throughout its jaws.

facts.statement: The molar-like teeth of Pakasuchus were complex enough to fit together and slice food like mammalian teeth.
facts.quote: The molar-like teeth show a level of complexity that matches that of mammals, being able to occlude, or fit with one another, and provide sharp shearing edges for slicing food.

facts.statement: Pakasuchus uniquely lost body osteoderms while retaining them on its tail among crocodyliforms.
facts.quote: The loss of osteoderms on the body and retention of them on the tail is unique among crocodyliforms.

facts.statement: Pakasuchus originally thought to be from the mid-Cretaceous (105 million years ago), but is now considered to have lived in the late Cretaceous (Cenomanian to Campanian).
facts.quote: Pakasuchus is originally considered to lived approximately 105 million years ago, in the mid-Cretaceous, but later age of site is reconsidered to the late Cretaceous, Cenomanian to Campanian instead.

facts.statement: Pakasuchus was an active terrestrial animal, like other notosuchians.
facts.quote: Like all notosuchians, it was an active terrestrial animal.

facts.statement: Pakasuchus was likely an herbivore with dentition as complex as modern herbivorous lizards.
facts.quote: Pakasuchus was probably an herbivore; its dentition was at least as complex as those of modern herbivorous lizards.

facts.statement: The lack of body armor in Pakasuchus may have been an adaptation to lighten its body for an active terrestrial lifestyle.
facts.quote: The relative lack of osteoderms on the body may have been an adaptation for an active terrestrial lifestyle, as it would have lightened the animal.

facts.statement: Pakasuchus's long legs and slender build likely made it more agile.
facts.quote: The long legs and slender build would also have made Pakasuchus more agile.

facts.statement: Pakasuchus is classified as a genus of notosuchian crocodyliform.
facts.quote: Pakasuchus is a genus of notosuchian crocodyliform

facts.statement: Pakasuchus belongs to the suborder Notosuchia.
facts.quote: subordo: Notosuchia

facts.statement: The parent group of Pakasuchus is the family Candidodontidae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Candidodontidae

facts.statement: Pakasuchus lived from the Cenomanian to the Campanian stages, between 100.5 and 72.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Cenomanian to Campanian (100.5 to 72.2 million years ago)

facts.statement: The name Pakasuchus means "cat crocodile" because its skull resembles that of a cat.
facts.quote: Pakasuchus means "cat crocodile" (paka meaning "cat" in Kiswahili) in reference to its catlike skull.

facts.statement: Pakasuchus's teeth are so mammal-like that isolated specimens could easily be mistaken for mammal teeth.
facts.quote: In fact, the teeth are so similar to those of mammals that it has led paleontologist Greg Buckley to state "If only isolated teeth had been discovered, without the skull, it is very likely that some of the molariform teeth would have been mistaken for a mammal's."

facts.statement: It is debated why Pakasuchus retained heavy osteoderms on its tail while losing them from its body.
facts.quote: However, the retention of osteoderms on the tail is hard to explain, as they would have been quite heavy.

rejected.statement: Pakasuchus had large sharp teeth at the front of its jaws and broad molar-like teeth at the back.
rejected.quote: There are large, sharp teeth near the front of the jaws, and broad molar-like teeth at the back of the mouth.
